segments.narration: Two massive warships vanished in the Arctic with 129 men. In 1845, HMS Erebus and Terror set sail to map the Northwest Passage. Then, total silence.
Search parties discovered frozen graves on Beechey Island and a handwritten note on King William Island explaining the ships were trapped in ice.
For nearly 170 years, searchers scanned millions of square miles without finding either ship. Were they looking in the completely wrong direction?
In 2014, underwater archaeologists finally discovered HMS Erebus intact on the ocean floor, followed by HMS Terror in 2016. Their locations matched accounts passed down by Inuit historians.
Inuit hunters had described the wreck in Terror Bay for generations before sonar proved them right. Why did it take searchers 170 years to finally listen?

verdicts.claim: Sir John Franklin's expedition with 129 men aboard HMS Erebus and HMS Terror departed in 1845 to map the Northwest Passage.
verdicts.note: The article states that Sir John Franklin departed in 1845 with 129 officers and men aboard HMS Erebus and HMS Terror to traverse the Northwest Passage.

verdicts.claim: Search parties discovered frozen graves and a handwritten note on King William Island explaining the ships were trapped in ice.
verdicts.note: The handwritten note (Victory Point note) explaining the ships were trapped in ice was found on King William Island, but the crew members' buried graves were located on Beechey Island.
verdicts.correction: Search parties discovered frozen graves on Beechey Island and a handwritten note on King William Island explaining the ships were trapped in ice.

verdicts.claim: Both lost warships remained undiscovered by Western searchers for nearly 170 years.
verdicts.note: The ships were abandoned in 1848 and discovered in 2014 and 2016, which is approximately 166–168 years later.

verdicts.claim: Archaeologists discovered the wreck of HMS Erebus in 2014 and HMS Terror in 2016.
verdicts.note: The article confirms that the wreck of Erebus was located in 2014 and Terror was found two years later in 2016.

verdicts.claim: Inuit oral history accurately identified Terror Bay as the location of HMS Terror long before modern sonar confirmed it.
verdicts.note: The article mentions that HMS Terror was found in Terror Bay, but it does not mention Inuit oral history regarding Terror Bay or modern sonar.
